The transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (TV-ICD) has long been the gold standard for the prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD). However, intravascular leads are associated with significant acute and long-term complications, such as pneumothorax, cardiac perforation, venous occlusion, pocket or systemic infections, and lead failure [1, 2]. To address these limitations, the entirely subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed [1]. By utilizing an extrathoracic lead placed subcutaneously, the S-ICD avoids the risks inherent to transvenous lead placement, offering a valuable alternative for many patients [3].

The clinical efficacy and safety of the S-ICD were initially established in pivotal trials and prospective registries [2]. Following the initial Food and Drug Administration (FDA) investigational device exemption (IDE) trial, the European EFFORTLESS registry confirmed these findings in a real-world setting, demonstrating high rates of successful defibrillation and a low incidence of lead-related complications over long-term follow-up [4, 5]. The landmark PRAETORIAN trial, a randomized, head-to-head non-inferiority trial comparing the S-ICD to the TV-ICD, provided definitive evidence [6]. Over a median follow-up of 4 years, the S-ICD was shown to be non-inferior to the TV-ICD with respect to the composite primary endpoint of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [6]. This established the S-ICD as a first-line therapy for patients without an absolute pacing indication [7, 8].

Proper patient selection remains critical for S-ICD success. Because the S-ICD cannot deliver chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), or anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP) for ventricular tachycardia (VT), candidates must not have indications for these therapies [9]. Furthermore, because the S-ICD relies on far-field surface electrocardiogram (ECG) signals rather than intracardiac electrograms, it is susceptible to cardiac oversensing, particularly of T-waves (T-wave oversensing, TWOS) [10, 11]. To minimize inappropriate shocks due to TWOS, candidates must undergo pre-implantation ECG screening using a manual or automated template system [12]. Advancements in screening, including the use of multisurface ECG screening, have significantly reduced the failure rate of screening vectors [13]. Additionally, the clinical implementation of the PRAETORIAN score—a tool designed to predict the risk of vector failure and inappropriate shocks based on chest radiographs—has refined patient risk-stratification [14].

Historically, inappropriate shock rates were higher in S-ICD cohorts than in TV-ICD cohorts, primarily due to TWOS and supraventricular tachycardias (SVT) [15]. To mitigate this, manufacturers developed advanced sensing filters and software. The introduction of the SMART Pass filter, designed to attenuate low-frequency signals like T-waves without affecting VF detection, significantly reduced inappropriate shock rates [16]. Moreover, programming has evolved to include dual-zone configurations (a conditional zone and a shock zone) and higher rate cut-offs. The UNTOUCHED trial demonstrated that contemporary S-ICD devices programmed with high-rate zones and the SMART Pass filter achieved inappropriate shock rates as low as, or lower than, those historically observed with TV-ICDs [17, 18].

The implantation technique for the S-ICD has transitioned from a three-incision method to a simplified two-incision technique, reducing procedural time and improving cosmetic outcomes [19]. Furthermore, intermuscular placement of the pulse generator (between the latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior muscles) has emerged as an alternative to subcutaneous placement, yielding superior cosmetic results, lower pain scores, and potentially lower defibrillation thresholds (DFT) [20, 21]. Defibrillation testing (DFT), once considered mandatory, is increasingly being questioned. The PRAETORIAN-DFT trial was designed to evaluate whether omitting DFT testing is non-inferior to performing it during S-ICD implantation, pointing toward a more streamlined procedural workflow [22].

Infection remains a serious complication, though the management of S-ICD infections is notably safer because extraction does not carry the risk of systemic bacteremia or endocarditis associated with transvenous lead extraction [23, 24]. Large registry data have further supported the long-term safety profile of the S-ICD, showing low complication rates in diverse real-world settings [25].

The S-ICD is particularly advantageous in pediatric and congenital heart disease patients, in whom venous access is often limited or complex [26]. It is also highly beneficial for patients with end-stage renal disease on dialysis, who are at exceptionally high risk for venous stenosis and systemic infections [27]. In older cohorts, the S-ICD remains a safe and effective option [28]. Looking ahead, the main limitation of the S-ICD—the lack of ATP—is being addressed through modular cardiac rhythm management (CRM) systems [29]. Recent clinical trials have demonstrated the feasibility and safety of combining the S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker. In this setup, the leadless pacemaker communicates wirelessly with the S-ICD to deliver ATP when ventricular arrhythmias are detected, effectively bridging the therapeutic gap [30].

In conclusion, the S-ICD has transitioned from a niche technology to a mainstream alternative for sudden cardiac death prevention. Ongoing advancements in hardware, software, and implantation techniques continue to enhance its safety profile and expand its clinical utility.
